exclusions: No entry recommends killing, poisoning, trapping, drowning, burning or destroying the subject, and no entry describes a method by which a listener could do so.
No entry calls the subject vermin, filth, a plague, an enemy or an infestation, and no entry frames a living thing as deserving to die.
No medical, veterinary or pesticide advice of any kind: no dosage, no treatment, no product, no brand, and no first aid beyond saying that a professional is the right person to ask.
No invented facts, invented figures, invented studies, invented quotations or invented experts; say plainly where the evidence stops rather than filling the gap.
No specific title, author, journal, institution or database is cited by name; describe the kind of source instead, so nothing is attributed to a work that may not say it.
No living private individual is named, described or spoken for, and no gardener, scientist or neighbour is invented to carry an anecdote.
No claim that a subject is harmless when it is not, and no claim that it is dangerous when the evidence does not support that; state the real risk once, plainly, and move on.
No hooks, cliffhangers, teasers, countdowns or references forward to a later chapter; every chapter stands on its own and resolves inside itself.
No startling turn, no sudden threat, no raised voice and no passage written to make a listener open their eyes; this pack is written for someone falling asleep.
No modern political framing, no campaigning language, and no instruction to the listener to act, buy, plant, join or stop doing anything.
No entry describes an animal in pain, dying, dismembered or being destroyed; predation is stated in one plain sentence and the chapter then moves to what it means for the garden.
No entry treats a species as universally dangerous on the strength of one incident, and no entry repeats a bite, sting or disease claim without the actual frequency behind it.
prompt_context:
Each episode follows one animal that lives in or around an ordinary house or garden, and each chapter is one part of what that animal actually does. Begin a chapter by naming plainly what it is about, in the first sentence, so a listener who wakes in the middle always knows where they are. The whole pack is written on one assumption: almost everything a listener already believes about these animals is either wrong or wildly out of proportion, and the correction is the interest, not a scolding.

Tell each chapter as observation rather than argument. Say what the animal does, how it does it, what it costs the animal, and what it does for everything else in the garden. Where the animal genuinely causes a problem — a slug in a lettuce row, a mouse in a kitchen, a mole in a lawn — concede it fully and early, put a real number on it if the slot supplies one, and let the rest of the chapter be about the animal rather than the complaint. A pack that only defends its subjects is not worth listening to.

Risk is stated once and honestly. Where a bite, a sting, a bacterium or a parasite matters, give the real frequency and the real severity in one plain sentence, name who it actually affects, and do not soften it or dramatise it. Where a fear is unsupported, say so with the same flatness, and say where the belief came from if that is known.

Nothing in this pack tells a listener to kill anything, and nothing tells them how. Where a chapter reaches a practical point, it is a courtesy — a gap in a fence, a glass and a card, a lid on a water butt, a light switched off, a log left lying — never a treatment, a product or a dose. Give no medical, veterinary or pesticide advice at any point.

Name real species, places and periods plainly. Never name a living private individual, never invent a scientist or a neighbour to carry a story, and describe the kind of evidence a chapter rests on rather than citing a specific title, author or institution.

This is a sleep compilation before it is anything else. Keep the tempo even and low the whole way through, keep the volume flat, let each chapter resolve rather than hand over to the next, and never write a sentence designed to make a listener open their eyes. A listener who falls asleep in the first chapter must have lost nothing they were promised.

evidence_expectations: Ground each chapter in the kind of source named by its slot, and describe source types rather than citing any specific title, author, institution or database.

Say in every chapter whether the point rests on field observation, on a controlled experiment, on long-run survey data, on a historical record or on a tradition, and never let those four blur together.
Where a widely repeated belief about the subject is wrong, correct it plainly and early in the chapter rather than saving the correction for the end.
Where the evidence is genuinely thin or contested, say so in the chapter itself and give the competing readings rather than choosing one.
Give numbers only when the slot supplies them, state what they are counting, and never make a figure more precise or more dramatic than the evidence allows.
Treat a folk use, a traditional remedy or a piece of garden lore as a claim with a history, never as a demonstrated fact, and say what has actually been tested.
When a chapter states a bite, sting or disease risk, give the frequency and the affected group in the same sentence, so the number and the fear arrive together.
compatibility_rules: Pair with the sleep history compilation formula for the long form; this pack assumes long, even chapters with no tension carried between them and no build across the episode.
Pair with the natural world explainer formula for the short form; the same twenty slots then become twenty short sections rather than twenty chapters.
Use one subject per episode and never mix two, so an episode is one creature or one plant followed all the way round rather than an anthology.
The twenty slots of a subject may be drawn in any order, because each is self-contained; an episode that wants a shape should end on the closing slot rather than opening with it.
Do not pair with a formula that promises a reveal, a ranking or a countdown; nothing in this pack is written to be withheld.
